inline.s: The next day I gathered the officers of the various halls who had stayed behind on the mountain and discussed preparing a feast to thank the various protectors of the Dharma. I asked what the monastery still kept in store. The prior, Ruojian, replied: ‘There is no silver or money at all; of rice there are only a few measures left, and the storehouses are wholly empty.’ I sighed and said: ‘I have been away from the mountain not yet five months; how has the monastery come to such a pass?’ Ruojian said: ‘After the master left, the mountain was no longer like a Vinaya hall; everyone was thinking of going off elsewhere. And Master Mishi, every day, enjoyed sumptuous offerings (eating the best) with nothing coming in, and so what was stored has been used up. It is like using a limited supply of dead water, lacking a living spring, and so we have come to this state. And as for me, I could not decide anything.’ When the protectors heard this, they all knit their brows and were very displeased at heart. I said: ‘This return to the monastery is indeed very different from my return from the army camp last time. Simply go along with conditions; there is no need to worry!’ Gradually, people from near and far who came seeking the precepts grew more and more. I said to them: ‘The mountain is thin and poor and bitter. To add people to feed, we can only add a ladle of water; there is no rice to add. Those who cannot endure this hardship, please go elsewhere.’ They all were willing to stay on the mountain, and not one went elsewhere. From the eighth year of the Shunzhi reign, in every winter and summer season, the assembly within and without gathered together in one hall, reciting the Buddha-name for seven days and seven nights without pause, still eating only one bowl of gruel at midday, with no further meal after noon. This rule has been handed down and followed ever since, without change. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month, the day of self-reflection, in accordance with the scriptural regulations and ritual, an Ullambana offering was set up, and all the abbot’s money and goods were distributed in full to the assembly, to repay the profound kindness of parents — established as a constant and unchanging rule.

In the ninth year of the Shunzhi reign, the land south of the Yangtze suffered locusts and drought; not a blade of grass grew, and the common people went hungry and starving. The old and young, men and women, of the villages all came up the mountain seeking food. They were not entirely beggars; among them were also those who held fields, and at one go they came in groups of one or two hundred. I told the sangha to reduce their own rations to relieve them. One day around noon, the number who came was several times the usual, and the halls, courtyards, and corridors were filled with people. I seized the opportunity to instruct them, saying: ‘Everyone today, having no alternative, has come up the mountain. Each of you should look at the causes from the past. Because in former lives you did not believe in the Three Jewels, and being miserly and greedy were unwilling to give alms to the poor, you have drawn upon yourselves today’s retribution. Today I shall gather contributions from the assembly and give each of you three coins. I too shall give each of you one coin of my own. You must all recite the Buddha-name in your mouths and receive this with both hands, to make offering on your behalf and to plant a pure field of merit, so that in the future you may all be free from the suffering of poverty.’ Having thus taught them, at once the sound of the Buddha-name rose like thunder. I then ordered a monk to sweep the storehouse completely clean; the rice obtained was cooked into a meal, and after everyone had eaten his fill at will, they all went off reciting the Buddha-name. By this, the monastery had no rice left even for the following morning. On the next morning there was only a pot of plain boiled water for the meal, and by evening the layman Huang Junfu of Jiangning sent ten measures of rice to the mountain.

In the middle of the second month of the tenth year, a nun of Hanyang Prefecture in Chuzhou named Xinwen, already fifty years old and resolved to observe the precepts, led her nine disciples on a boat, fearing neither the distance nor the dangers of the road, and came to Huashan. The ten of them entered the monastery and begged for three months’ residence, offering sixty measures of rice and twenty taels of silver. Seeing that their intent was sincere and their words earnest, I took pity and consented. When the day came to set out a feast and offer to the assembly, she would not enter the hall to bow to the monks. When the meal was over, I gathered the assembly, had her called, and said: ‘You have roused your heart to come from afar to learn the precepts. Why do you not enter the dining hall and bow to the monks? The Vinaya rule stipulates that a bhikshuni, even at the age of a hundred, should bow to a bhikshu of the first summer (a bhikshu who received the full precepts only a year ago). Today you yourself are arrogant and haughty, showing great disrespect toward the monks — this is not the conduct of one who studies the precepts.’ She said: ‘Wherever I have been, in the Chu region, if there were a good spiritual friend, I would go and set a feast and offer to the assembly. The abbots there all treated me with the courtesy of a guest, and did not require me to bow.’ I said: ‘They are greedy for offerings and are corrupting the Dharma. Seeing a nun who can make offerings, they honor her as their own mother, wishing to obtain even more abundant offerings. They are worms in the lion’s body, not true spiritual friends. Though Huashan at present is thin and poor and bitter, I would rather run out of grain and miss meals than dare to violate the Vinaya rules to seek gain. The feast set up today may be counted for the monastery’s own use. The silver spent I return to you in full; and the rice you brought, place it in the lower courtyard and take it away with you. Go elsewhere!’ Not understanding the principle, she took the silver, led her disciples, went down the back mountain, and lodged in the quiet room of the Water-Out Cave. At this a disciple, Gutang, came to the abbot’s room and said: ‘She has come from afar, and the monastery’s storehouse is empty. Master, exercise a little kindness and take her in. For one thing, it keeps her from losing her resolve for the Way; for another, the assembly will have half a month’s provisions.’ My face darkened and I said: ‘If one is willing to practice truly, the assembly will naturally not go hungry with hanging bowls. To establish the Dharma, it should be precisely in such a time of bitter poverty and hardship, in word and deed. A Vinaya master carrying out the precepts — can he violate the holy ordinances for the sake of gain?’ Gutang, blushing, bowed and withdrew.

After three days, the nun Xinwen again led her disciples up the mountain, and they all knelt outside the abbot’s door, weeping and saying: ‘When we were in Chu we were truly befuddled to such a degree — it was really our own arrogance and slighting of the monks. We humbly beg the master, out of his compassion, to allow us to repent. From now on, all your teaching and instruction we shall follow and carry out one by one!’ The heads of the various halls also pleaded on their behalf. Therefore I had them go to the Deer-Mountain Manor, where a boundary was drawn for them to carry out the summer residence, and I dispatched an acarya and others to go there every half-month to give them instruction, and to explain for them the fundamental Vinaya text of our order. From this matter onward, I formed the resolve to compile the one scroll, The Proper Standard for Instructing Bhikshunis, and to circulate it.

In the first part of the eighth month, the monk Huiyi of the rear hall, a man of the Chu region who had long studied in the Chan school, came up the mountain to rely upon me, studying the precepts. One day the monastery brought out the stored scriptures to air them. Huiyi turned the leaves of the Sutra of the Pratyutpanna Samadhi. The next day he said to me: ‘The Pratyutpanna Samadhi in the scriptures is the essential substance of pure-karma practice, and the hardest of all to carry out.’ I said: ‘Earlier, at the five platforms of the north, I too heard a good spiritual friend instruct that to practice the Pratyutpanna Samadhi one must not sit or lie down, but must stand for ninety days. Later, coming to this place, I read the Collected Conduct of the Vinaya Ancestor Daoxuan of the Southern Mountain and learned that the ancestral master had long practiced this method, and that after him, those who practiced it became few. If one can only let go of the body, naturally one can do it.’ So I fixed the twentieth day of the eighth month as the start, and in the abbot’s room, emulating the worthies of old, I practiced the ninety days; I made a vow to follow in the footsteps of the patriarchs, declining all affairs and entering the retreat. Having completed the term on the twenty-first day of the eleventh month, I again, in the autumn of the twelfth year of the Shunzhi reign, practiced ninety days a second time. I rejoice that I had such good conditions as to let me plant this pure cause twice. Yet I am deeply ashamed of my heavy hindrances, and that I did not gain deep benefit.

As for my relying on the Vinaya rules to reform some of the earlier expedient methods and to hold them strictly in accordance with the Dharma; and my compiling the Proper Standard of the Vinaya to distinguish what is false and spread it abroad; and all these matters of the conditions for guiding and transforming beings; as well as establishing a precept altar to transmit the precepts, setting an example for later generations; purchasing field and mountain to support the sangha; and all the various works of building, great and small — all these undertakings were to complete and enrich the plans that the former elder could not finish after he redirected his course. By these I repay his profound kindness to me in bestowing upon me the milk of the Dharma of the precepts. This is also the real substance of my decades of painstaking effort, with an iron spine bearing up to sustain the Buddha’s work of spreading the Dharma. Here, not fearing to be tediously long-winded, I have set it before you all, one item after another. These are all things that the acarya Liyan and the great disciples who long attended me witnessed with their own eyes. But one must know that all that has form returns to illusion. Now, recalling the former events, it is only a dream; therefore I have titled it A Wandering Talk of a Dream. I add a gatha:
A dream southward for many a year, through peril and hardship I came;
And now you ask of my southern route — I answer still in a dream’s own frame.
